content: Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic primarily used to treat intestinal parasitic infections, such as amebiasis. It works by inhibiting the growth of parasites in the intestines. Additionally, it may be used in conjunction with a specialized diet to manage hepatic encephalopathy, a serious brain condition caused by elevated ammonia levels in individuals with liver disease. This medication is not effective against viral infections, such as the common cold or flu. When taking paromomycin, it is essential to adhere to the prescribed dosage schedule and complete the full course of treatment, even if symptoms improve after a few days. This ensures the infection is fully eradicated and reduces the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Side Effects Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and heartburn. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to oral thrush or new vaginal yeast infections. Serious allergic reactions are rare but possible. If you experience severe symptoms, such as difficulty breathing or swelling, seek immediate medical attention. Precautions Before starting paromomycin, inform your healthcare provider if you are allergic to this medication, other aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin), or any inactive ingredients in the formulation. This medication may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. During pregnancy, paromomycin should only be used when clearly necessary, and its safety during breastfeeding is not well established. However, due to its poor oral absorption, it is unlikely to harm a nursing infant. Drug Interactions Paromomycin may interact with other medications, altering their effects or increasing the risk of side effects. For example: Paromomycin and succinylcholine: Increased risk of apnea due to pharmacodynamic synergism. Avoid or use alternative drugs. Paromomycin and tacrolimus: Both drugs increase nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Monitor closely. Paromomycin and teicoplanin: Increased risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Use caution and monitor. Paromomycin and tenofovir DF: Increased nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Paromomycin may elevate tenofovir levels by reducing elimination. Paromomycin and thiamine (oral): Paromomycin may reduce thiamine levels by altering intestinal flora. Paromomycin and live typhoid vaccine: Paromomycin reduces the vaccine's effectiveness. Wait until antibiotic treatment is complete before administering live bacterial vaccines. Special Considerations Paromomycin is poorly absorbed when taken orally, with nearly 100% of the drug excreted unchanged in feces. This minimizes systemic exposure and reduces the likelihood of fetal harm during pregnancy. However, caution is advised in individuals with ulcerative bowel lesions, as inadvertent absorption may lead to renal toxicity. Prolonged treatment may result in fungal or bacterial superinfections. If new infections caused by resistant organisms occur, appropriate measures should be taken. Constant monitoring of the patient is essential during therapy. If adverse effects or new infections arise, consult a healthcare professional immediately. Storage and Handling Store paromomycin at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication as instructed by your pharmacist. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into drains unless directed to do so. Overdose In the event of an overdose, seek emergency medical attention immediately. In the U.S., call 911 or contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. Important Notes This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about paromomycin. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider for personalized guidance regarding this medication and your specific health needs.
